title: Tomb Raider
shortDescription: Core Design's atmospheric 3D cinematic adventure that introduced British archaeologist Lara Croft to world culture.
historicalSignificance: Introduced one of gaming's most recognizable cultural icons, Lara Croft, while delivering a groundbreaking grid-based 3D locomotion system that made spelunking, swimming, and puzzle-solving feel authentically dangerous and cinematic.

editorialContent.overview: Conceived by Toby Gard at Core Design in Derby, UK, Tomb Raider launched in October 1996 initially on the Sega Saturn before storming PlayStation and PC. Following British aristocrat-archaeologist Lara Croft on a globe-trotting hunt for the Atlantean Scion, the game discarded arcade run-and-gun conventions in favor of tense architectural exploration, isolating ambient soundscapes, and calculated athletic maneuvers.
editorialContent.gameplay: Built upon an invisible 3D tile-grid, Lara's locomotion demands strict measurement: walk steps, run-up jumps, ledge grabs, backflips, and precision swan dives. Players explore ancient subterranean tombs across Peru, Greece, Egypt, and Atlantis, solving physical counterweight puzzles while defending against wolves, bears, raptors, and a terrifying Tyrannosaurus Rex.
editorialContent.technicalInnovation: Core Design constructed a fully 3D camera and environment engine that supported dynamic vertical cavern spaces, underwater 360-degree swimming physics, and cinematic orchestrations triggered dynamically by spatial triggers.
editorialContent.culturalImpact: Lara Croft transcended video games to become a global 1990s media icon, appearing on the cover of The Face, starring in high-budget Hollywood feature films, and reshaping mainstream attitudes toward female protagonists in entertainment.
editorialContent.preservationNotes: Preserved via original Saturn and PS1 optical media, PC DOS executables, and modern source reimplementations such as OpenLara.

awards: BAFTA Interactive Entertainment Award for Best Game
